text: Build an LRU cache with a fixed capacity. get of a key returns its value, or negative one. put inserts or updates. When it's full and a new key comes in, you drop the one used least recently. Both operations should be constant time on average.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — does a get count as a use? So if I read a key, does that move it away from the chopping block?
Yes. Both get and put count as a use.
Good. And a get that misses — does that count as a use too?
No. A miss just returns negative one. Nothing changes.
That helps. Are there any constraints on the input size?
Capacity is between one and three thousand, with up to two times ten to the fifth calls.

Here's the thing that shapes the whole design: this problem asks for two things at once, and no single data structure gives me both. A hash map finds a key fast, but it has no order, so it can't tell me who's oldest. A list keeps the order of use, but it can't find a key without walking it. So I want both, side by side — and what ties them together is that the hash map stores the address of the list node. One lookup, and I'm holding the node.

Let me run through the example. Capacity two. Put one, put two — now it's full. Then get one returns one, and that read makes key one the newest. So when put three comes in, the one that gets dropped is key two, not key one. That single get decided who lived.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would keep just a hash map with a timestamp per entry. That's correct and easy — I'd use it as my reference when I test — but eviction scans every entry, so it's linear in the capacity. A vector for the order is no better: moving one item shifts everything after it, and every index saved in the map now points at the wrong element.

This problem reminds me of the classic hash map plus doubly linked list pairing. One thing worth flagging — it has to be doubly linked. Even with the node in hand, a singly linked list can't unhook it without the node before it, and finding that means walking from the head. The constant-time lookup gets cancelled out by a linear unhook. With prev pointers, a node can unhook itself.

Here's the plan. One: the list holds the order, oldest to newest, and the map holds key to node address. Two: a use unhooks the node and attaches it at the newest end. Three: an eviction takes the node at the oldest end and removes it from both structures. The invariant is that the list is always sorted by last use — nothing computes it, every operation just maintains it. It costs two structures and two pointers per node, to turn eviction from a scan into a single step.

One thing worth flagging about the plan: whenever a node enters or leaves, both structures must change together. Unhook a node but forget the key, and the map keeps a ghost entry. Erase the key but forget to unhook, and the list keeps an orphan that can never be evicted. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?
Sounds good. Go ahead.

Alright, let me code this up. I'll write the hand-rolled list first, so the mechanics are visible. Two dummy nodes, left and right, sit at the ends, so prev and next are never null — that's why remove and insert have zero if statements. A get hit unhooks the node and re-attaches it before right, the newest end. A put on an existing key updates the value and moves it the same way. Otherwise, if the cache is full, the victim is simply left's next. One thing worth flagging — Node stores the key, which looks redundant. It isn't: at eviction I reach the node from the list side, and only the node knows which key to erase from the map.
You said there's a shorter version. Show me.

Right. std list is already a doubly linked list, so I drop my Node class and both dummies, and the map stores a list iterator instead. The front is the newest end. The one call that makes this work is splice: passing the same list as source and target moves a node inside the list in constant time. Two details. First, after splice the map needs no update — splice only rewires links, the node never moves, so the stored iterator stays valid. Second, the order of the eviction lines matters. pop back returns nothing and frees the node, so I copy the key first. Swap them, and the evicted key stays in the map pointing at freed memory — AddressSanitizer reports heap-use-after-free at the next splice.

Let's dry-run the code on the official example, capacity two, with the std list version, where front is newest and back is oldest. Expected: one, negative one, negative one, three, four. The row that matters is get one: before it, key one sits at the back, next to go. That single get splices it to the front, so put three drops key two instead. One read changed who was evicted. After that nothing touches key one, so it drifts back and put four drops it. That matches.

Let's also test corner cases. Capacity one: every new key evicts the previous one. A get on an empty cache finds nothing and returns negative one. A get miss returns early and leaves the list untouched. A put on an existing key updates and moves it, with no eviction. Beyond that, I'd cross-check both versions against the timestamp brute force, comparing the full newest-to-oldest order after every operation — because a missing move-to-front keeps the contents right and only gets the order wrong.

Let me think about complexity here. Both operations are constant time on average: one hash lookup plus a fixed number of pointer writes. The list half is worst-case constant; the average comes only from the hash map. Space is linear in the capacity — one node and one map entry per key. The worst case is every put being a new key on a full cache, so every call evicts. That's still constant, because the victim is always the node at the oldest end.

Oh, one more thing — two notes on the versions. Memory: version one never deletes the evicted node. LeetCode won't catch it, but the leak grows with evictions — capacity ten with a hundred thousand distinct keys leaks a hundred thousand and two nodes, about two point three megabytes. std list frees its own nodes, so nothing is left outstanding. And a speedup: on a hit, put can edit the value in place and splice, instead of erase plus push front — about eight times faster on hitting puts. It all works because list iterators stay valid; a vector breaks that.

Good. Three things stood out. You explained why the list has to be doubly linked — a singly linked one cancels out the fast lookup. You caught that splice doesn't move the node, so the stored iterator survives, and tied that to why a vector can't work here. And you knew pop back frees the node before you can read it, so the key has to be copied first — a bug that only blows up later, somewhere else. Good work.
